Surah al-Mujadila (The Pleading Woman)

It is so named because, since it concerns the seeking of truth and correctness, it resembles the disputation of the prophets and of the Qur'an; and for this reason God "heard" the words of its companion. Thus said al-Mahayimi.

It is Medinan, and its verses number twenty-two.

(p-٥٧٠٥) In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿God has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to God, and God hears your exchange of argument. Indeed, God is Hearing and Seeing.﴾

﴿God has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to God, and God hears your exchange of argument. Indeed, God is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ Imam Ahmad narrated: "From Aisha, she said: Praise be to God, whose hearing encompasses all voices. The woman who pleads (al-mujadila) came to the Prophet ﷺ speaking to him, while I was in a corner of the house, and I could not hear what she was saying! So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿God has indeed heard﴾ to the end of the verse." Al-Bukhari narrated it in suspended form (mu'allaq). In a narration of Ibn Abi Hatim: "From Aisha, that she said: Blessed is He whose hearing reaches everything. I was hearing the speech of Khawla bint Tha'laba, and some of it was hidden from me, while she was complaining of her husband to the Messenger of God ﷺ, saying: O Messenger of God! He has consumed my youth, and I have spent my womb for him; but now that my age has grown old and my children have ceased, he has made me unlawful to him (zihar). O God, I complain to You." She said: "She had not yet left when Gabriel descended with this verse: ﴿has heard﴾," etc. Ibn Kathir said: It is also said of her: Khawla bint Malik ibn Tha'laba, and she may be diminutized as Khuwayla. There is no contradiction between these reports; the matter is close. In al-'Inaya: The meaning of His saying ﴿God has indeed heard﴾ etc. is: He accepted her words and responded to them, as in "God hears those who praise Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), by metaphor through the relation of causality, or by metonymy. End of quotation.

And His saying:

﴿and complains to God﴾, i.e., the pleading woman complains to God of the distress she has from the zihar of her husband towards her, and asks Him for relief.

(p-٥٧٠٦) The meaning of ﴿your exchange of argument﴾ is your returning of speech concerning this incident. That is because zihar in the Jahiliyya was a man's divorce of his wife: once he uttered it, he never returned to his wife again. The complainant hoped that it would not sever the bond of marriage. The Prophet ﷺ did not decide the matter for her until revelation descended which settles the dispute. Then God, exalted is He, revealed concerning it His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 58, verse 2:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Those among you who divorce their wives by zihar (saying "you are to me like the back of my mother") — they are not their mothers. Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them. And indeed they say an objectionable word and a falsehood. But indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

﴿Those among you who divorce their wives by zihar﴾ means the saying of a man to his wife when he is angry with her: "You are to me like the back of my mother," meaning: in the prohibition of riding (intercourse).

﴿They are not their mothers﴾ means: their wives whom they have made like their mothers through zihar are not their mothers; that is, by this saying they do not become like their mothers in permanent prohibition.

Al-Mahayimi said: "They are not their mothers in reality, nor in their legal status by way of metaphor, since metaphor does not necessitate that it be in the legal status of reality, except by reversing realities, but these realities are not reversed."

﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾ means: therefore wives are not to be likened to mothers in prohibition. ﴿And indeed they say an objectionable word﴾ means: a saying that sensible people reject and noble people shun.

﴿And a falsehood﴾ means: something untrue with no reality, because it involves attaching the wife to the mother, which contradicts what the marital bond requires. ﴿But indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ means: toward the sins of His servants, when they repent from them and turn back in repentance, so He does not punish them for them after repentance.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 58, verses 3–4:**

(p-5707) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[3–4] ﴿Those who divorce [by zihar] from their wives and then retract what they said, [the penalty] is the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do. And whoever does not find [a slave], then [the penalty is] fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another. And whoever is not able, then [the penalty is] feeding sixty needy persons. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. And these are the limits of Allah, and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3–4]

[4] ﴿Those who divorce [by zihar] from their wives and then retract what they said﴾: i.e., they return to the expression of zihar (zihar, the pre-Islamic formula of divorce by likening a wife to one's mother) a second time, so that "qawl" is taken in its literal sense. Or they resolve to have intercourse with them and to have sexual relations with them, desiring to make them lawful again after having made them forbidden. Thus "qawl" here means "that which was said." ﴿[The penalty is] the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿And whoever does not find [a slave], then [the penalty is] fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another. And whoever is not able, then [the penalty is] feeding sixty needy persons. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. And these are the limits of Allah, and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]

Imam Ahmad narrated from Yusuf ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, from Khuwaylah bint Thaʿlabah, who said: "By Allah, it was about me and about Aws ibn al-Samit that Allah revealed the beginning of the surah al-Mujadila." She said: "I was with him, and he was an elderly man whose character had deteriorated and who had become irritable. He came in to me one day and I argued with him about something, and he became angry and said: 'You are to me like the back of my mother.' She said: Then he went out and sat in the assembly of his people for a while, then came in to me, and behold, he wanted me for himself. I said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Khuwaylah! You will not reach me, after you have said what you have said, until Allah and His Messenger judge between us with a judgment.' She said: He pounced on me, and I resisted him, and I overpowered him with what a woman overpowers a weak old man, and I threw him off me." He said: "Then I went out to one of my neighbours, (p-5708) and borrowed her clothes, then I went out until I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and I sat before him and mentioned to him what I had encountered from him, and I began to complain to him about the bad character he had shown." She said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ began to say: 'O Khuwaylah! Your cousin is an elderly man, so fear Allah regarding him.' She said: By Allah, I had not moved from my place before the Qur'an was revealed concerning me. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was overcome by what usually overcame him, then it passed from him, and he said to me: 'O Khuwaylah! Allah has revealed concerning you and your companion...' Then he recited to me: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1], up to His words: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]. She said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'Tell him to free a slave.' She said: I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! He does not have anything with which to free a slave!' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' He said: I said: 'By Allah! He is indeed an elderly man, and he has no capacity for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty needy persons, a wasq of dates.' She said: I said: 'By Allah! O Messenger of Allah, he does not have that either.' She said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Then we will assist him with a faraq of dates.' She said: I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I too will assist him with another faraq.' He said: 'You have done right and well. Go and give it in charity on his behalf, then treat your cousin well.' She said: So I did that." This was also narrated by Abu Dawud, and in his narration it is "Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah." There is no contradiction, as stated earlier, for the Arabs often diminutivize proper names.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When a man said to his wife in the Jahiliyyah: 'You are to me like the back of my mother,' she became forbidden to him in Islam. The first to make zihar in Islam was Aws, and he had a paternal cousin as a wife called Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah. He made zihar from her, and he was dismayed, and said: 'I do not see you except that you have become forbidden to me,' and she said to him the same. He said: 'Go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' So she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found with him a woman who was combing his hair, and she informed him. He said: 'O Khawlah! We have not been commanded regarding your matter with anything.' Then Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ, and he said: 'O Khawlah! Rejoice!' She said: 'Good news.' He said: Then he recited to her: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1], up to His words: ﴿the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾." She said: (p-5709) "And what slave do we have? By Allah! We do not find a slave other than myself!" He said: "﴿And whoever does not find [a slave], then [the penalty is] fasting two consecutive months﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]." She said: "By Allah! Were it not that he drinks three times a day, he would lose his sight." He said:

"﴿And whoever is not able, then [the penalty is] feeding sixty needy persons﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]." She said: "From where? It is nothing but one meal to the next!" He said: So he (the Prophet ﷺ) supported him with half a wasq, thirty ṣāʿ, and the wasq is sixty ṣāʿ, and he said: "Let him feed sixty needy persons, and let him return to you."

Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is good and strong, but its context is unusual, and something similar has been narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah."

Notes:

al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: In this verse are the ruling of zihar; that it is among the major sins; that it applies only to wives, not to non-Muslim women; that in it, returning [to the statement] entails an expiation; that intercourse is forbidden before it; and that the expiations are in order: freeing a slave, then fasting two consecutive months, then feeding sixty needy persons. Malik derived from His words "from you" (minkum) that a disbeliever does not fall under the ruling. He derived from His words ﴿from their wives﴾ that it is valid regarding wives and concubines, since the word "women" includes them.

Ibn Jarir, Dawud and a group derived from His words ﴿then retract what they said﴾ that the retraction which requires expiation is that one returns to the expression of zihar and repeats it.

Whoever permitted freeing a non-Muslim woman in the expiation of zihar derived this from the unrestricted (muṭlaq) term "slave."

Whoever held that zihar is only valid by likening [a wife] to the mother's back specifically, and not to the other limbs, and not merely by saying "like my mother," and specifically to the mother and not to grandmothers or other close relatives by blood, fosterage or marriage, such as the father or son and the like, derived this from the apparent sense of the verse. Whoever said that a wife's zihar against her husband has no ruling, because He, exalted is He, restricted zihar to men, held this view. Whoever said that the zihar of a slave is valid, because of the generality of "those who," held this view. Whoever said that the enjoyments (other than intercourse) are permitted, on the basis that they are not included in the word "touching," held this view. Whoever said that intercourse and similar acts are permitted before feeding [the poor], if one is expiating by it, because the phrase ﴿before they touch one another﴾ is not mentioned in it [i.e., in the feeding], held this view.

(p-5710) In the verse there is a refutation of those who made the expiation obligatory by the mere utterance of zihar without considering the retraction. The basis of what he said is that he made the "return" to be his act in Islam after its prohibition.

In it there is also a refutation of those who sufficed with feeding one needy person sixty days.

The end.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]: i.e., that explanation or instruction of the rulings is so that you may affirm Allah and His Messenger by accepting their laws and refraining from the false speech of the Jahiliyyah.

By His words, exalted is He: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4] is meant those who deny His obligations and His limits which He has explained. Thus "disbelief" is taken in its literal sense, or it refers to those who transgress them, and the title "disbelief" is used to intensify the warning and deter them.

The discussion on the Exalted saying:

[5] ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated, just as those before them were humiliated. And We have sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: in violating His limits (hudud) and obligations (fara'id). Its root is from al-muhaddah (opposition), meaning mu'adah (hostility), because each of the two opponents is in a limit other than the limit of the other.

﴿will be humiliated﴾ means: will be disgraced. ﴿just as those before them were humiliated﴾ refers to the disbelievers of the earlier nations.

﴿And We have sent down clear signs﴾ Ibn Jarir said: meaning detailed proofs and firm signs, which indicate the realities of Allah's limits. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾ means those who deny those signs and reject them.

Note:

Some have explained: ﴿oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ as meaning they establish or choose limits other than the limits of the two.

The commentator on it (muhashshi) said: In this is a severe warning for kings and wicked rulers who have set down matters contrary to what the Sharia has defined, and called them law (qanun).

He also said: The gnostic of Allah, Shaykh Baha' al-Din, may Allah sanctify his spirit, composed a treatise on the disbelief of one who says: one acts by the law and the Sharia when he sets them against each other, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and religion has reached a degree of perfection that does not admit of completion. And when the river of Allah comes, the river of Ma'qil ceases. End of his words.

It is not hidden that the blanket application of disbelief to this alone, without detail, is open to question, because it is from the excess of the extremist jurists, whose statements on takfir were rejected by many of the leading scholars, for takfir is no small matter. The truth in this matter is that a law which demolishes the texts of the Sharia that do not admit of interpretation, and nullifies, or abrogates them, is indeed disbelief and misguidance, and no one holds to it or relies upon it except the apostates and deniers. As for what is not expressly stated — I mean what is not decisive in its domain — from a clear verse, or a mutawatir report, or a consensus in the derivative rulings and the ijtihadi matters that have been recorded, then opposing these in favour of a just law is not considered misguidance or disbelief, because it is not opposition to the Sharia in any way; for the Sharia is what Allah and His Messenger have legislated, and the matter in it has been made firm and explained with a clarity that removes all confusion, not what the jurists differ over, whose source is ijtihad and the exercise of opinion; for that has no protection from error, however high the rank of its holder, since infallibility belongs only to the text of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Often the derivative rulings of the jurists resemble the articles of law, and for this reason some later scholars wrote a book matching the statutory articles to the jurisprudential derivatives, because the source of all of them is one: opinion, ijtihad, and the consideration of public interest.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah has a book on this theme called "al-Siyasa al-Shar'iyya", and likewise his student (p-5712) the Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, which is broader. Najm al-Din al-Tufi also has a treatise on al-Masalih al-Mursalah (unrestricted public interests), which we compiled from his commentary on the Forty Hadith of al-Nawawi. Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam reduced the derivative rulings of jurisprudence in his Qawa'id to two principles: the consideration of public interests and the averting of harms.

Qadi Zakariyya said: Some have argued that all of them return to the attainment of benefits.

Al-Shatibi said in al-Muwafaqat: The Lawgiver intended by legislation the establishment of interests in both the Hereafter and this world, and that they be interests absolutely; therefore its placement in that manner must be perpetual, universal and general across all kinds of obligation and all obligated persons in all circumstances.

Najm al-Din al-Tufi said: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm" requires the consideration of interests, affirmatively and negatively, and of harms negatively, since harm is the mafsadah; when the Sharia negates it, the affirmation of benefit, which is the maslahah, becomes necessary, because they are contradictories with no intermediary between them. Then, the strongest evidences are the text and the consensus, and they either agree with the consideration of interest or oppose it. If they agree, then so be it, and there is no dispute, for the three proofs have agreed upon the ruling: the text, the consensus, and the consideration of interest derived from his saying, peace be upon him: "There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm." If they oppose it, it is obligatory to give precedence to the consideration of interest over them by way of specification and clarification of them, not by way of usurping them or nullifying them, just as the Sunnah is given precedence over the Qur'an by way of clarification. End of his words. The conclusion of his speech is worthy of review, along with our annotations upon it, so investigate, and do not be a captive of imitation, but rather one of those who listen attentively while being a witness.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, though they have forgotten it. And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it﴾ i.e., Allah has encompassed it in knowledge, and nothing of it has escaped Him. ﴿though they have forgotten it. And Allah is, over all things, Witness﴾ i.e., Watcher, who knows it and is not absent from Him. The word "Day" (yawm) is in the accusative, governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur). The preceding of the report about the vastness of His knowledge, glory be to Him, serves as a preparation for what follows of the prohibition against secret conferring in sin, as a warning and a deterrent. He has emphasized this by detailing His knowledge, out of concern for what is forbidden and what is warned against, in His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? There is no private conversation between three but that He is their fourth, nor [between] five but that He is their sixth, nor [between] fewer than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? There is no private conversation between three but that He is their fourth, nor [between] five but that He is their sixth, nor [between] fewer than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ "Najwa" is a verbal noun whose meaning is speaking privately. It is derived from "al-najwah" (an elevated part of the ground), because a secret is kept safe from others, as if it has been lifted from the lowland of being apparent to the height of concealment, by way of metaphor.

Al-Shihab said: Closer to this is the statement of al-Raghib, because those who speak secretly withdraw to an elevated spot of the ground. Or it is from "al-najah" (salvation). As for the specification of the two numbers, it is either due to the particular occurrence: a group of hypocrites, with this number, gathered to vex the believers; or because private consultation (tanaji) is for counsel, and its minimum is three, since consultation necessarily requires two who are like disputants, and a third who mediates between them. The reason for adding five to three is that five is the first of the levels above it in oddness, so both are mentioned to point to the lesser and the greater. Then he generalized the ruling afterwards with His saying:

﴿Nor [between] fewer than that﴾, i.e., like two, ﴿or more﴾, i.e., like six and what is above it, ﴿but that He is with them wherever they are﴾, i.e., He knows what occurs between them in whatever place they settle, because His knowledge of things is not by spatial nearness, so that it would vary with differing places. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: He is above the Throne, and His knowledge is with them wherever they are.

Ibn Kathir said: More than one scholar has reported a consensus that the intended meaning of this verse is the accompaniment of His knowledge, exalted is He. There is no doubt that this is what is intended.

Imam Ahmad said: He opened the verse with knowledge and closed it with knowledge.

Note:

The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that Allah, exalted is He, is in every place. Imam Ibn Hazm in "al-Fisal" refuted them, saying that the words of Allah, exalted is He, must be taken in their apparent sense unless another text, or a consensus, or a necessity of the senses prevents taking them in their apparent sense. We know that whatever is in a place occupies that place and fills it, and takes on its shape, or the place takes on its shape, and one of the two must necessarily be the case. We also know that whatever is in a place is finite by the finitude of its place, and has six or five directions finite within its place, and all these are attributes of body. Since what has been mentioned is established, we know that His saying, exalted is He:

(p-5715) ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16] ﴿And We are closer to Him than you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no private conversation between three but that He is their fourth﴾, is only about management of that and encompassing it, and encompassing alone is a necessity, since nothing beyond that is implied. Also, their saying "in every place" is an error, because by the implication of this statement He would have to fill all places, and what is in the places would be within Him, exalted is Allah above that, and this is impossible. If they say: He is in them, unlike the case of something settled in a place.

It is said to them: This is not conceivable, and no proof stands for it. End.

It has already been mentioned, in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], a discussion on the meaning of accompaniment by Ibn Taymiyyah; refer to it in Surah al-Hadid.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[8] ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conferring, then they return to what they were forbidden from, and they confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger? And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah has not greeted you, and they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?" Sufficient for them is Hell; they will burn in it, and wretched is the destination.﴾

﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conferring﴾ Mujahid said: They are the Jews.

﴿Then they return to what they were forbidden from, and they confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ That is: by that which is sin and aggression against the believers, and mutual counsel in opposing the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu al-Su'ud said: Mentioning him, upon him be prayer and peace, by the title of Messenger between the two addresses directed at him is for the increase of their reproach and the magnification of their disobedience.

﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah has not greeted you﴾ That is: from their saying, "As-sam 'alayka" (death be upon you), or from what Islam abrogated of the greetings of the Jahiliyyah, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And peace upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 181]

(p-5716) ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ That is: for the blameworthy secret conferring, or for the distortion in the greeting, mockingly and derisively. That is: Why does He not hasten His punishment for us for that, if Muhammad were truly His Messenger? Allah, exalted is He, said:

﴿Sufficient for them﴾ That is: it suffices those who say that for their punishment. ﴿Hell; they will burn in it, and wretched is the destination.﴾

Then Allah, exalted is He, forbade the believers and warned them against committing in their secret conferring what those others had committed, by His saying:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9–10] ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult privately, do not consult privately in sin and aggression and disobedience of the Messenger, but consult privately in righteousness and piety. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿Indeed, private consultation is from Satan, that he may grieve those who believe, but he cannot harm them at all, except by Allah's permission. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10]

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult privately, do not consult privately in sin and aggression and disobedience of the Messenger, but consult privately in righteousness﴾, i.e., in obedience to Allah and that which brings you closer to Him, ﴿and piety﴾, i.e., avoiding what is sinful, ﴿and fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾, i.e., He will recompense you for what you have earned, of what He has counted against you.

Then Allah, exalted is He, encouraged the believers not to be concerned about the private consultation of their enemies, and that it does not harm them as long as they are persistent in His commands and rely upon Him, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, private consultation is from Satan﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10], i.e., the private consultation that He has censured. The lam here is for specification (al-'ahd), i.e., it is Satan who adorns this private consultation with evil and who drives toward it.

﴿That he may grieve those who believe, but he cannot harm them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10], i.e., Satan, or the aforementioned private consultation, ﴿at all, except by Allah's permission﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10], i.e., by His will, ﴿and upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10], i.e., by proceeding on His path, remaining steadfast upon His command, and awaiting victory in its wake.

(p-5717) A subtlety:

Al-Qashani said: They were forbidden from private consultation because private consultation is a connection and union between two people in a matter that is specific to them, which no third party shares. When souls come together and connect, there is mutual support and reinforcement, each strengthening and confirming the other in that which is the cause of their gathering, due to the special character of the collective condition, which does not exist in individuals. So if they are wicked, they consult privately in evil, evil increases in them, and the meaning for which they consult privately grows stronger among them through connection and gathering. For this reason, after the prohibition, He said:

﴿and they consult privately in sin﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8], which is the vice of the bestial faculties, ﴿and aggression﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8], which is the vice of the irascible faculties, ﴿and disobedience of the Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8], which is the vice of the rational faculty, through ignorance and the dominance of satanic nature. Do you not see how, after this verse, He forbade the believers from private consultation in these mentioned vices, and commanded them to consult privately in good, so that they may strengthen themselves through the collective condition and increase in it? He said: ﴿but consult privately in righteousness﴾, i.e., the virtues which are the opposites of those vices, of the good deeds and excellent acts specific to each of the three faculties, ﴿and piety﴾, i.e., abstaining from the categories of the aforementioned vices. End quote.

Ibn Kathir said: The Sunnah has come forth prohibiting private consultation where it causes harm to a believer. Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you are three, let not two consult privately apart from the third, for that would grieve him." Agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

(p-5718) And from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you are three, let not two consult privately apart from the third except with his permission, for that would grieve him." Narrated by Muslim alone.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[11] ﴿O you who believe, when you are told, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; Allah will make room for you. And when you are told, "Rise up," then rise up. Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿O you who believe, when you are told, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; Allah will make room for you.﴾ This is an instruction from Him, Exalted is He, to the believers regarding good conduct in the etiquette of gatherings, namely that a person should make room for his brother and move aside to widen the space for him.

Al-Shihab (al-Alusi) said: Its connection to what precedes it is clear, because when He forbade secret conferring and private whispering, it was understood from this that sitting with the company was permitted, so He mentioned its etiquette and made the reward for their compliance a widening (fusha) for them in what they wish to make room for, namely place, provision and breadth of heart.

Ibn Kathir said: This is because the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, as came in the authentic hadith: "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise. And whoever eases the lot of one in difficulty, Allah will ease his affairs in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother." There are many similar examples of this.

Qatadah said: This verse was revealed concerning gatherings of remembrance (dhikr). That was because when they saw one of them approaching, they were reluctant to make room for him in their gatherings with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah commanded them that some of them should make room for others.

(p-5719) ﴿And when you are told, "Rise up,"﴾ that is: stand up to make room, or rise to higher places in the assemblies, or stand up from the gathering of the Messenger when you are commanded to get up from it, and do not weary him by lingering in it. ﴿Then rise up. Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.﴾ That is: He will raise the believers who comply with His commands and those of His Messenger, and the people of knowledge who act upon it and follow its requirements in accordance with their knowledge, by degrees, both in this world and in the Hereafter.

Al-Nasir said: Since He knew that people of knowledge deserve, in their own estimation and in the estimation of people, that their gatherings be elevated, He singled them out for mention at the point of recompense, so that it would be easy for them to give up the elevated status they have in a gathering, out of humility before Allah, Exalted is He. End of quotation.

This, as al-Shihab said, is among the unseen matters (mughayyabat) of the Qur'an, because of what has appeared from such people throughout the ages of competition for elevated places in gatherings and love of being at the forefront.

In the words of al-Zamakhshari there is something indicating that this is the mention of the specific after the general (min 'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), glorifying it: it is placed after it as though it were a different category, as in ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. For this reason the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) was repeated in the wording. By "knowledge" is meant the knowledge of what is indispensable of sound beliefs and righteous deeds.

Notes (tanbihat):

The first: In "al-Iklil" it is said: The verse indicates the recommendation (istihbab) of conduct in gatherings of knowledge and remembrance, and every gathering of obedience.

The second: From the command to make room is understood the prohibition of having a person removed so that another may sit in his place. On the authority of Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man should not remove a man from his seat and then sit in it himself; rather, make room and widen the space." Narrated by Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

(p-5720) And on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A man should not remove a man from his seat and then sit in it; rather, make room, and Allah will make room for you." Narrated by Imam Ahmad. In another narration with the wording: "A man should not stand up for a man from his seat; rather, make room, and Allah will make room for you." Imam Ahmad alone narrated it.

Ibn Kathir said: The jurists have differed concerning the permissibility of standing up for one who arrives, in several opinions. Among them are those who permitted it, citing the hadith: "Stand up for your master (sayyid)."

Among them are those who prohibited it, citing the hadith: "Whoever loves that men should stand before him as he stands, let him take his seat in the Fire."

Among them are those who made a distinction, saying: It is permitted upon arrival from a journey, and for a ruler within the area of his authority, as indicated by the story of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, for when the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned him to judge over Banu Qurayzah, and he saw him approaching, he said to the Muslims: "Stand up for your master." And that was only so that his judgment would be more binding, and Allah knows best. As for making it a habit, it is one of the customs of the 'ajam (non-Arabs). It has come in the Sunan that there was no person more beloved to them than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and yet when he came they would not stand for him, because they knew how much he disliked that. End of quotation.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in a fatwa of his on this matter: It was not the custom of the early generation (al-salaf) in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his rightly-guided successors to make a habit of standing as many people do today. Rather, Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: There was no person more beloved to them than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when they saw him they did not stand for him, because they knew how much he disliked that. However, they sometimes stood to greet someone returning from absence, as was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he stood for 'Ikrimah," and "he said to the Ansar when Sa'd ibn Mu'adh arrived: 'Stand up for your master.'" Sa'd had been ill in Medina, and he had gone to Banu Qurayzah, east of Medina.

(p-5721) What people should do is accustom themselves to following the early generation in what they were upon in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), for they are the best of generations, the best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad. No one should turn away from the guidance of the best of creation and the guidance of the best generations to something inferior to it. The one who is obeyed should make this clear to his companions, so that when they see him they do not stand for him, nor should he stand for them, except at the customary meeting. As for standing for one who comes back from a journey or the like, greeting him, it is good.

And if it is the custom of people to honour the one who comes by standing, and if that were abandoned, he would believe that this is a diminishing of his right or an intention to lower him, and he would not know the custom that agrees with the Sunnah, then the better course is that he be stood for, because that is a reconciliation of hearts and the removal of hatred and resentment. As for the case where the custom of the people is in agreement with the Sunnah, there is no harm to him in leaving it, and this standing is not the standing mentioned in his (ﷺ) words: "Whoever is pleased that people should stand before him, let him take his seat in the Fire." That refers to their standing while he is seated, not standing when he arrives. For this reason they distinguished between saying "I stood up to him" (qumtu ilayhi) and "I stood up for him" (qumtu lahu). One who stands for the one who arrives is equal to him in standing, unlike standing for one who is seated. It is established in Sahih Muslim that when the Prophet (ﷺ) led them in prayer while seated during his illness, and they prayed standing, he commanded them to sit, and said: "Do not exalt me as the non-Arabs exalt one another." So their sitting, rather than standing in prayer while he was seated, was so that they would not resemble the non-Arabs who stand for their great ones while they are seated. The sum of this is that what is right is following the custom and character of the early generation, and striving within one's capacity. Whoever does not regard this as the custom, or does not know that it is the custom, and for whom omitting to treat him with the respect people customarily show would cause a greater harm, then he should avert the greater of the two corruptions by accepting the lesser, just as it is obligatory to achieve the greater of two benefits by forgoing the lesser. End of the words of Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him on behalf of Islam and the Muslims with good.

The third: Ibn Kathir said: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan al-Basri and others that they said regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿when you are told, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room﴾, that it means the assemblies of war. They said: The meaning of His words ﴿and when you are told, "Rise up," then rise up﴾ is: rise up for fighting.

(p-5722) Qatadah said: ﴿And when you are told, "Rise up," then rise up﴾ means: when you are called to good, respond.

Muqatil said: When you are called to prayer, rise up for it.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: When they were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in his house and wished to leave, each of them loved to be the last of them to leave his presence, and this would sometimes burden him, peace be upon him, when he had a need. So they were commanded that when they were told to depart, they should depart, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are told, "Return," then return﴾ [al-Nur: 28]. End of quotation.

There is no contradiction among these sayings, because each of them is an explanation of the general term by one of its instances. What it applies to is indicated by its inclusion of that, not that one of them alone is meant to the exclusion of the others; therefore nothing of this kind is to be feared. Such things are common in the tafsir of the early generation regarding many verses, and all of it is among matters on which there is no disagreement, as we have explained many times.

The fourth: In "al-Iklil" it is said: Some people said: The meaning of ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees﴾ is that Allah will raise the believers among you, the scholars, by degrees above others. Therefore He commanded making room for their sake, and in this there is evidence for elevating scholars in gatherings and making room for them away from the places of honour. End of quotation.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, precede your private consultation with a charity. That is better for you and purer. But if you do not find [anything to give], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, precede your private consultation with a charity﴾ i.e., give charity before you confide in him (secret consultation, al-munajah) concerning some of your affairs.

﴿That﴾ i.e., the advance giving.

﴿is better for you﴾ i.e., for your own souls, because of the multiplication of reward and recompense in it, and the fulfilment of the right of brotherhood, by returning to those in need with consolation and enrichment.

﴿and purer﴾ i.e., for your own souls, from the vice of miserliness (al-bukhl) and stinginess (al-shuhh), and from love of wealth and preferring it, which may be a mark of the hypocrites. It seems that the command to give charity mentioned was revealed so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite: the believer's soul is generous with faith in whatever state it is, while the other chokes on it, even in the most dire times. Most of the commands of this surah concern giving charity, urging on the stingy and driving the believers forward. ﴿But if you do not find﴾ i.e., what you might give in charity before your consultation with the Messenger ﷺ, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ i.e., toward whoever does not find it, since He does not embarrass him nor constrain him, out of His mercy.

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[١٣] ﴿Do you fear, before your private conversation with the Messenger, to offer charity? So since you did not do it, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness, then establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

﴿Do you fear, before your private conversation, to offer charity?﴾ That is: did you fear poverty and destitution from offering charity? This is a rebuke, indicating that one should not fear such a thing, since giving and spending brings replacement, just as the shadow follows the object, by the true promise of Allah.

﴿So since you did not do it﴾ That is: you did not do what you were recommended to do, offering charity, and it was difficult for you. ﴿And Allah has turned to you﴾ by granting you leave not to do it, lifting the hardship in accordance with your apprehension. ﴿Then establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ That is: do not neglect prayer, zakat, and the rest of the acts of obedience, for that will instill in you the disposition of goodness and virtue. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ That is: He will recompense you according to it.

Note:

In "al-Iklil" (the book of al-Suyuti): His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿When you consult the Messenger...﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12], the verse, is abrogated (mansukhah) by the one after it, and in this is evidence that abrogation (naskh) is permissible without a substitute, and that it occurs, contrary to those who deny that. End of quote.

Apparently the principle of the matter is that the widely known source of the claim of abrogation is what Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, who said: Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, there is a verse which no one acted upon before me, and no one will act upon after me: ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger...﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12], etc." He said: "It was made obligatory, then it was abrogated."

And from him also, he said: "They were forbidden to consult the Prophet ﷺ until they gave charity, and none consulted him except Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He offered a dinar and gave it in charity, then the concession concerning it was revealed."

And from Qatada: that it is abrogated, and it lasted only an hour of a day.

And from him also, he said: "The people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so much, to the point that they pressed him with questions, so Allah admonished them with this verse." A man would have a need of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ but could not fulfill it until he offered a charity before him, and this was hard upon them, so Allah revealed the concession after that: ﴿But if you do not find [anything], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12]

And from al-Hasan and Ikrima, they both said: ﴿When you consult the Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12], the verse, was abrogated by the one after it: ﴿Do you fear...﴾, the verse.

These reports and their like are the basis of those who claim abrogation, holding to their apparent meaning. We have previously stated in the introduction to the tafsir (exegesis), and in other places, that abrogation in the speech of the early generations (salaf) is broader than its technical meaning among later scholars (khalaf), just as the meaning of the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is broader than what is immediately understood. From this is Qatada's statement here: "Then Allah revealed the concession after that," for his intention is to make clear that the matter is not an obligation in the second verse, not that its revelation was delayed from the first; for that is impossible given the splendor of its noble arrangement. The principle regarding verses that establish a ruling is the continuity of their clauses and the coherence of their structure, for by it the magic of their eloquence and the excellence and completeness of their jurisprudence are perfected. As for those who held that abrogation does not occur in the revelation, they have several arguments concerning the verse:

(p-5725) The first: the statement of Abu Muslim: The hypocrites used to refrain from giving charity, and a group of the hypocrites abandoned hypocrisy and believed outwardly and inwardly, with true faith. So Allah, exalted is He, willed to distinguish them from the hypocrites, so He commanded giving charity before private conversation, so that those who truly believed would be distinguished from those who remained upon their original hypocrisy. And if this obligation was for the sake of this interest, which was limited to that time, then this obligation is necessarily limited to that time.

Al-Razi said: The essence of Abu Muslim's statement is that this obligation was limited to a specific end, so when that specific end was reached, it ceased; therefore this is not abrogation. And this statement is good, and there is no fault in it. End of quote.

The second: the statement of some of them: The basis of the claim of those who assert abrogation is their view that the command to offer charity is obligatory, and this is reinforced by His saying after it: ﴿But if you do not find [anything], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12], and His saying: ﴿So since you did not do it, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness﴾. For such wording is not used except for a matter whose obligation ends with its absence. The answer: there is no decisive proof that the command is for obligation; rather the apparent meaning is that it is for recommendation (nadb). And several things indicate this:

The first: His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿That is better for you and purer﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12], and this is used only for voluntary acts, not for obligatory ones.

The second: that if it were obligatory, its obligation would not have been removed by a speech connected to it, namely: ﴿Do you fear that you will offer charity...﴾ to the end of the verse.

The third: that His saying: ﴿So since you did not do it, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness, then establish prayer...﴾ etc., means: if you did not do what you were recommended to do, namely offering charity before consulting the Messenger, while Allah has returned to you with lightness and facilitation in what He legislated for you, and He did not deal with you as He dealt with the earlier nations, and did not burden you with anything He had made obligatory upon you. Therefore He recommended this matter to you and did not make it an obligation, as is His way of dealing with you in compassion and mercy. So establish prayer... etc. Thus His saying: ﴿and Allah has turned to you﴾ (p-5726) has come here in the sense of returning to lightness and ease for this nation, and turning away from treating it as He treated the previous ones; not in the sense of pardoning sins and forgiving transgressions. And this meaning has also come in another verse in Surah al-Muzzammil, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you [in mercy]﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], that is: He returned to you with lightness, and removed from you what was burdensome upon you. Its meaning in these two verses is not the pardoning of sins, since no sin had proceeded from them here. This is the summary of what those who held that abrogation is impossible have verified. And the truth, its strength is not hidden and the soul finds tranquility in it. And success is from Allah.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[14] ﴿Have you not considered those who have allied themselves with a people upon whom Allah has become angry? They are neither of you nor of them, and they swear by a lie while they know [it].﴾

﴿Have you not considered those who have allied themselves with a people upon whom Allah has become angry?﴾ means the hypocrites (munafiqun) who used to ally themselves with the Jews, give them sincere advice, and convey to them the secrets of the believers, as is explained by the verse: ﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite saying to their brothers who disbelieved from among the People of the Scripture...﴾ [al-Hashr: 11], to the end of the verse.

﴿They are neither of you﴾ means: not of the people of your religion and creed, O company of Muslims. ﴿Nor of them﴾ means: not of the Jews, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾ [an-Nisa': 143]. ﴿And they swear by a lie﴾ Ibn Jarir said: This refers to their saying to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah," while they were liars, not believing in him.

﴿While they know [it]﴾ means: the matter sworn to is a pure lie.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 58, verse 22:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan. Those - He has written within their hearts faith and supported them with a spirit from Him. And He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah - they are the successful.﴾

(p-5729) ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., who oppose and contravene their command. That is: you will not find a people who combine belief in Allah and the Last Day with loving the enemies of Allah and His Messenger. The purpose of the negation of finding is the negation of love, in the sense that it should not occur, and that it ought to be prevented and not found in any state, as an exaggeration in forbidding it, in warning against engaging in it, and in enjoining firmness in keeping away from and distancing oneself from the enemies of Allah, and guarding against mixing with and associating with them. He added to this emphasis and intensification with His saying: ﴿even if they were their fathers﴾, i.e., the fathers of those who show love. The pronoun in "were" refers to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. The plural is in consideration of the meaning of (man), just as the singular in what precedes it is in consideration of its wording.

﴿or their sons, or their brothers, or their clan﴾, i.e., for the requirement of faith is the abandonment of those who oppose. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those who do not love them. ﴿He has written within their hearts faith﴾, i.e., He has established it therein. ﴿And supported them with a spirit from Him﴾, i.e., with light, knowledge and gentleness, by which their hearts came to life in this world. He pointed to what they have in the Hereafter with His saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan. Those - He has written within their hearts faith and supported them with a spirit from Him. And He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah - they are the successful﴾, i.e., the prosperous and the triumphant, with the happiness of both abodes.

Remarks:

First: Among the likes of this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. And whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except when taking precaution against them in prudence. And Allah warns you of Himself. And to Allah is the final destination﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 28], and the verse. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your clan, the wealth you have acquired, a commerce you fear will decline, and dwellings you find pleasing are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and jihad in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people"﴾ [at-Tawbah: 24].

(p-5730) Second: Ibn Kathir said: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and others said: This verse, ﴿You will not find a people﴾ to its end, was revealed concerning Abu 'Ubaydah 'Amir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah when he killed his father on the day of Badr. And concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who that day intended to kill his son 'Abd al-Rahman; and concerning Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who killed his brother 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr; and concerning 'Umar, who killed a close relative of his from his clan on that day as well; and concerning Hamzah, 'Ali and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, who killed 'Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid ibn 'Utaybah that day. End of quotation.

We have explained repeatedly that what is meant by the occasion of revelation in such cases is the verse's applicability to these people and to what they did of firmness in the religion of Allah, in confrontation with corrupters, even if they were from the closest of relatives.

Ibn Kathir said: Of this kind is when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted the Muslims about the captives of Badr, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq advised that they be ransomed, so that what is taken from them would be a strength for the Muslims, and they are the paternal cousins and the clan, and perhaps Allah, exalted is He, would guide them. 'Umar said: I do not see what he saw, O Messenger of Allah! Let me kill so-and-so, a relative of 'Umar, and let 'Ali have 'Aqil, and let so-and-so have so-and-so, so that Allah may know that there is no love for the polytheists in our hearts.

Third: Ibn Kathir said: In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ there is a wondrous secret, which is that when they were angered at their relatives and clan for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, Allah compensated them with His being pleased with them, and made them pleased with Him by what He gave them of everlasting bliss, great success, and abundant favour.

Fourth: From His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ and His saying in another verse: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], it is understood that what is meant by them are those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger, who bar from His way, who openly display enmity and hatred. They are those whom He informed of earlier, that they confer secretly in sin, transgression and disobedience of the Messenger. So the verse includes the polytheists and the People of the Book who wage war against us and oppose us, i.e., those who are (p-5731) in a state of hostility toward us, and of keeping aloof from our affairs, in order to realize their opposition to us and to watch for an opportunity to harm us. As for the People of the Covenant (dhimmis) who live among us, those who have agreed to pay the jizyah to us, made peace with us, and submitted to our rulings and judgments, the verse does not include them, because they are not opposing us in the sense we have described. For this reason they have what we have, and what is upon them is upon us, and it is permissible to marry from among them, to partner with them, to trade with them, and to visit their sick. For the Prophet (ﷺ) visited a Jew, and offered him Islam, and he embraced Islam, as related by al-Bukhari.

It is incumbent upon the Imam to protect them, to prevent harm from reaching them, and to rescue their captives, because the rulings of Islam apply to them and their covenant is perpetual, so this obligation falls upon him just as it falls upon the Muslims, as in al-Iqna' and its commentary.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in Ighathat al-Lahfan, in refutation of the over-scrupulous who are not content with many of the permitted concessions: Among that is that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to accept the invitation of whoever invited him and eat his food, and a Jew hosted him with barley bread and rancid fat. The Muslims used to eat from the food of the People of the Book. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, stipulated the hospitality of whoever passed by them from the Muslims, and said: Feed them of what you eat. Allah, mighty and majestic, has permitted that in His Book. When 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to Syria, the People of the Book prepared food for him and invited him, and he said: Where is it? They said: In the church. He disliked entering it, and said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: Take the people. 'Ali took the Muslims, and they entered, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, began looking at the image, and said: Would it be wrong for the Commander of the Faithful to enter and eat! End of quotation.

The basis for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8], ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion and expel you from your homes and aid in your expulsion - [forbids you] from making allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 9].

(p-5732) Al-Sayyid Ibn al-Murtada al-Yamani said in Ithar al-Haqq, on the authority of the Imam al-Mahdi Muhammad ibn Mutahhar, peace be upon him, that the prohibited loyalty by consensus is that you love the disbeliever for his disbelief, and the disobedient for his disobedience, and not for any other cause, such as bringing benefit, warding off harm, or some good quality in him. There will come at the beginning of Surah al-Mumtahanah more on this, if Allah wills, exalted is He. And success is from Allah.
